full_judgment:
Salma Masud Chowdhury, J: This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 30.3.92 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Rajshahi in Family Appeal No.21 of 1989 arising out of the judgment and decree dated 3.9.1989 passed by the Family Court, Rajshahi in Family Court Case No.7 of 1987 should not be set aside and/or pass such other order or further order or orders as to this court may seem fit and proper. 

 4. The date for pre-emptory hearing was fixed on 24.8.1989 and an application for adjournment of the case was filed on behalf of both the plaintiff and the defendant on the ground that the well wishers of the parties were attempting to arrange a compromise between the parties and adjournment was thus necessary. The trial court rejected the application for adjournment by the order dated 24.8.89 and asked the parties to get ready for hearing on the ground that previously adjournments were taken on many occasions. Thereafter, the plaintiff adduced 3 witnesses on that day and on 3.9.89 the suit was decreed exparte to the effect that defendant would pay TK. 35,001/- as dower money and TK. 48,000/- as maintenance allowance amounting to TK.83,001/- in total. 

 5. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the trial court the defendant preferred appeal in the court of District Judge, Rajshahi being Family Appeal No.21 of 1989 and the same was disposed of by the Subordinate Judge by his judgment and decree dated 30.3.92. The appeal was allowed in part and the defendant appellant was directed to pay TK.41,500.50, half of the decretal amount to the plaintiff respondent within 30 days, and after depositing the said amount on production of a receipt of the same to that court, the Family case shall revive or be restored to give the defendant appellant a chance to contest the case, otherwise the appeal will be treated as dismissed. 

 6. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree passed by the lower appellate court, the present petitioner filed this revisional application before this court and obtained the present Rule. 

 7. Mr. Asad Hossain Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant appellant petitioner submits that the petitioner totally denied the marriage with the plaintiff and the exparte judgment and decree of the trial court was bad for non-consideration of the joint application for adjournments on behalf of both the parties. He also submits that the judgment and decree of the courts below are absolutely illegal. The learned lawyer also submits that the Family Court did not comply with the mandatory provisions of section 10 and 13 of the Family Court Ordinance, 1985 to make effort to effect compromise or reconciliation between the parties and in view of that it would have been proper on the part of the lower appellate court to send the matter on remand to the trial court to rectify the error and also to give the petitioner an opportunity to cross examine the plaintiff witness and examine his own witnesses in his defence, but instead of that the appellate court gave direction for its restoration or revival with a condition. He further submits that the lower appellate court has no jurisdiction to get the matter restored and only the court before whom the exparte decree was passed had the jurisdiction to restore the case on an application filed by the defendant under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure but since it is not an application before the lower appellate court against the rejection of the restoration application under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure but rather an appeal was preferred challenging the exparte decree, the lower appellate court should have sent it back on remand. The learned lawyer further submits that the plaintiff opposite party is not entitled to past maintenance which she claimed before the Family Court along with her dower money and maintenance can only be allowed to her only from the date of institution of the suit before the Family court within 3 months after the decree for dissolution of marriage. In support to his contention he referred to a decision as reported in 43 D.L.R.(HC) page 301 and also section 278 of Molla's Principles of Mohammedan Law. He repeatedly submits that the defendant appellant petitioner was highly prejudiced by the exparte decree of the trial court as he could not get any opportunity to prove his case and it is necessary that the case be sent on remand. Lastly, the learned lawyer appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that the judgment and decree passed by the lower appellate court is not in accordance with the provisions as laid down in Civil Procedure Code, for revived or restoration of a case. 

 8. Mr. Subrata Saha, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-respondent opposite parties submits that the plaintiff was married to the petitioner by a registered Kabinnama which was not challenged by the defendant in any court of law and when the application for adjournment was rejected and the matter was taken up by the trial court on the same day, the plaintiff examined 4 witnesses to prove her case and the defendant willfully remained absent. The learned trial court fixed 3.9.89 for orders for enabling the defendant to examine the plaintiff's witnesses including his own, but he did not take any step and allowed the suit to be decreed exparte. The learned lawyer further submits that the defendant intentionally did not avail the opportunity to cross-examine the witnesses. The learned lawyer drew our attention to the observations of the lower appellate court where the court observed that the plaintiff proved her case by oral and documentary evidences where as the defendant sought time repeatedly and did not contest the trial seriously; it was further observed by the lower appellate court that the plaintiff has been suffering from paralysis. The learned lawyer submits that the father of the plaintiff died during the pendency of this Rule. He also submits that inspite of the observations and directions of the lower appellate court giving opportunity to contest the Family case and prove it in his favour by adducing evidence, the defendant appellant petitioner filed this revisional application on flimsy grounds in order to deprive the plaintiff from her rightful claim and the court below committed no illegality in passing the impugned judgment and decree and the same having not occasioned any failure of justice, the present Rule is liable to be discharged. 

 9. I have perused the revisional application along with the annexures filed by the defendant appellant petitioner and the affidavit-in-opposition filed on behalf of the plaintiff-respondent-opposite party and heard the learned lawyers appearing on both sides. It appears from the record of the civil revision that on 12.4.94 the rule was discharged for default as none appeared subsequently it was restored by the order dated 12.11.97. During pendency of the Rule the plaintiff respondent opposite party died and her mother, sisters and brother were substituted. It also appears that Rule was issued on a condition that the petitioner shall deposit a sum of TK.20,000/- by two installments and the petitioner duly deposited the money to Bangladesh Bank in compliance with this court's order. It appears that the plaintiff filed a suit before the Family Court claiming her dower money and maintenance allowances since 1978. It is evident from the order dated 24.8.89 that a joint application was filed before the Family Court for adjournment which was rejected by the court on the ground that adjournments were granted earlier on several occasions. 4 witnesses adduced by the plaintiffs were examined but the defendant did not appear and 3.9.89 was fixed for order and the defendant was also not present on that date and on consideration of the oral and documentary evidence the case of the plaintiff was allowed and suit was decreed exparte. It also appears that the plaintiff was suffering from paralysis and was seriously ill and died during the pendency of the Rule. The courts below believed the case of the plaintiff but for ends of justice, the lower appellate court directed the defendant to pay half of the decretal amount to the plaintiff within 30 days of the judgment and decree of the appellate court if he wants to contest the case before the Family court on restoration, otherwise the appeal shall be deemed to be dismissed. The lower appellate court has rightly given the order for restoration instead of the order of remand as claimed by the petitioner because the court while hearing Family appeals under Family Court Ordinance 1985 has no jurisdiction to send the case on remand to the trial court. Section 20 of the Family Court Ordinance 1985 clearly provides that save or otherwise expressly provided by or under this Ordinance, the provisions of the Evidence Act, 1872 (1 of 1872), and of the Code of Civil Procedure except sections 10 and 11 shall not apply to proceedings before the Family Courts. Thus the lower appellate court having no power to send the matter on remand before the trial court under Order 41 Rule 23 of the Code of Civil Procedure has rightly passed the impugned judgment reviving the matter on condition to make part payment of the decretal amount to the plaintiff by the defendant for ends of justice. The decision cited by the learned lawyer for the petitioner as reported in 43 D.L.R.(H.C.) page 301 to the effect that the wife is not entitled to past maintenance had been challenged before the Appellate Division and subsequently the view of the High Court Division was discarded by the Appellate Division which was reported in 48 D.L.R. (AD) page 110. It was held that by the Appellate Division that "although the view taken in Sarder Muhammad's case does not literally embrace the exposition of Hanafi Law in Baillie's Digest and in Hamilton's translation of Hedaya, and advances closer to the Shafi School of thought, we find that the advance by way of ijtihad has been made in the right direction, with strong reasons so far undisputed and of course within the bounds of Sunni Law. We therefore find no reason why the enunciation of law on past maintenance made in 1964 by the Lahore High Court and governing the field for 32 years without being reversed by either this Court or Pakistan Supreme Court, on the contrary being reaffirmed twice by the Pakistan Supreme Court, should be overlooked or discarded without demolishing the reasons given therefor. We hold therefore that the High Court Division was wrong in denying past maintenance to the appellant on the ground of a lack of prior agreement and further hold that past maintenance is available to the appellant."
